```{r setup, include=FALSE}
library(learnr)
library(tidyverse)
library(Lahman)   # install.packages("Lahman") if you don't have this
library(broom)
library(modelr)
theme_set(theme_bw())
wae <- read_tsv("data/WikiArt-Emotions-All.tsv.gz") |>
  mutate(year4 = substring(Year, 1, 4),
         year4_num = as.numeric(year4))
People_clean <- filter(People, !is.na(weight))
set.seed(2939394)
```

## Overview

When you first meet a data set, you do not yet know what questions to ask of it.
**Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA)** is the process of finding out -- and once we
spot a relationship, a **model** lets us describe it with a number. In this
lecture:

* What EDA is, and how it differs from inference
* Describing **variation** in a single measurement (the ECDF, histograms,
  density plots)
* Describing **covariation** between measurements (conditional distributions,
  stratifying, smoothing)
* Modeling the **conditional mean** with linear regression, polynomials, and
  loess

## What is EDA?

**Exploratory Data Analysis** is the process of learning about a data source and
generating questions about it. It is **informal** and **data-driven**:

* Generate questions about your data.
* Search for answers by visualizing, transforming, and modeling.
* Use what you learn to refine your questions and ask new ones.

The goal at this stage is *quantity* of questions over polish. Getting a clean
answer is nice, but not yet required.

## EDA vs. inference

EDA is about the data set **in front of you**.

**Inference** is about making informed guesses about data you **did not**
observe -- estimating, testing hypotheses, or predicting with the aid of a
statistical model.

EDA helps you generate the questions that inference can then answer more
forcefully.

## John Tukey, father of EDA

<center>

![John Tukey](images/John_Tukey.jpg)

</center>

>* The best thing about being a statistician is that you get to play in
>  everyone's backyard.
>* The first task of the analyst of data is quantitative detective work.
>* Far better an approximate answer to the right question, which is often vague,
>  than an exact answer to the wrong question, which can always be made precise.

## The big question: variation

If every observation had the same value, one number (or one category) would
describe the whole data set. Usually they differ -- they exhibit **variation**,
and describing it is the central task of EDA.

* The **distribution** of a measurement is the set of possible values and how
  often each occurs.
* We start with one measurement at a time (its **marginal distribution**), then
  look at how measurements vary *together* (**covariation**).

## Reminder: types of data

How we describe a distribution depends on the kind of measurement:

>* **Nominal / categorical**: one of a fixed set of categories.
>* **Ordinal**: categories that can be ordered.
>* **Quantitative**: numeric values, possibly infinitely many.

## A quick aside: your tools are the tidyverse

We are about to compute summaries with `count`, `group_by`, `summarize`, and
`ggplot`. In the last lecture we saw that a **package** bundles up functions and
data to share -- and here is something we have kept quiet all term: almost every
function you have used comes from a package, and they belong to one family, the
**tidyverse**. Calling `library(tidyverse)` loads them all at once:

| What you have been doing                                                | Package     |
|-------------------------------------------------------------------------|-------------|
| Reading data files (`read_csv`)                                         | `readr`     |
| Storing data in tibbles (`tibble`)                                      | `tibble`    |
| Transforming data (`filter`, `mutate`, `group_by`, `summarize`, joins)  | `dplyr`     |
| Reshaping and tidying (`pivot_longer`, `pivot_wider`)                   | `tidyr`     |
| Plotting (`ggplot`, the geoms)                                          | `ggplot2`   |
| Working with strings (`str_*`)                                          | `stringr`   |
| Working with factors (`fct_*`)                                          | `forcats`   |
| Iterating (`map`, `map_dbl`)                                            | `purrr`     |

The tidyverse is a *collection* of packages, each owning one part of the
workflow, all designed to fit together. The data-transforming functions in
particular -- `filter()`, `select()`, `mutate()`, `group_by()`, `summarize()`,
`arrange()`, and the joins -- are the **`dplyr`** package, which we lean on
constantly. With our tools named, let's use them to explore.

## Categorical distributions: counts

When observations fall into a fixed set of values, a table of counts describes
the distribution:

```{r}
count(People, bats)
```

This is the same as grouping and counting:

```{r}
People |> group_by(bats) |> summarize(n = n())
```

## From counts to proportions

Counts are easier to compare as **proportions** -- the share of the data set in
each category:

$$\frac{\text{number in group}}{\text{size of data set}}$$

```{r}
People |> group_by(bats) |> summarize(n = n()) |> mutate(prop = n / sum(n))
```

## A proportion is a mean

Here is a useful idea we will lean on. Suppose we want the proportion of players
weighing 200 lbs or less. The condition `weight <= 200` is a vector of
`TRUE`/`FALSE`, and R treats `TRUE` as 1 and `FALSE` as 0, so the **mean of the
condition is the proportion** that satisfy it:

```{r}
People_clean |> summarize(mean(weight <= 200))
```

## Quantitative: the ECDF

For a numeric measurement there are too many distinct values to count, but we
can describe the **empirical cumulative distribution function** (ECDF):

$$\hat F(x) = \text{proportion of observations} \le x$$

This is exactly the "mean of a condition" idea, evaluated at every `x`.

```{r}
ggplot(People_clean, aes(x = weight)) +
  stat_ecdf() +
  ylab("Proportion less than or equal to x")
```

## Reading the ECDF

The ECDF answers "what proportion is in a range?" by subtraction. The proportion
between 200 and 250 lbs is $\hat F(250) - \hat F(200)$:

```{r}
People_clean |> summarize(mean(weight <= 250) - mean(weight <= 200))
```

## From ECDF to histogram

Chopping the range into bins and reporting the count in each gives a
**histogram** -- a more familiar picture of the same distribution:

```{r}
ggplot(People_clean, aes(x = weight)) + geom_histogram(bins = 30)
```

## Choosing bin width

The picture depends on the bin width. Too few bins hides structure; too many is
all noise:

```{r}
ggplot(wae, aes(x = `Ave. art rating`)) + geom_histogram(bins = 1)
ggplot(wae, aes(x = `Ave. art rating`)) + geom_histogram(bins = 500)
ggplot(wae, aes(x = `Ave. art rating`)) + geom_histogram(bins = 50)
```

Always try a few bin widths before trusting a histogram.

## Density plots

A histogram also depends on *where* the bins start. A **density plot** averages
over all starting positions, giving a smooth estimate; its smoothness is set by
a **bandwidth** (analogous to bin width):

```{r}
ggplot(wae, aes(x = `Ave. art rating`)) + geom_density()
```

```{r}
ggplot(wae, aes(x = `Ave. art rating`)) + geom_density(bw = 0.03)  # too noisy
```

## What to look for

With our goal of understanding variation, scan each plot for:

* A **typical** value -- where is the center?
* **Clustering** -- one peak or several (multiple modes)? Tight or spread out?
* **Where the variation lives** -- more spread among small values or large?
* Anything **surprising** -- gaps, spikes, outliers worth investigating.

## Missing values

Real data is rarely complete. R marks missing values with `NA`, and `is.na()`
detects them. Parsing `wae`'s `Year` to a number produces some:

```{r}
wae |> summarize(missing_year = mean(is.na(year4_num)))
```

Ways to handle missingness:

* **Drop** the rows (`drop_na()`, or `na.rm = TRUE` in many functions).
* **Impute** a simple guess (e.g., the mean of the observed values).
* **Model** the missing values from the other variables.

Always notice *how much* is missing before deciding.

## Covariation

So far, one measurement at a time. The more interesting questions are about
**covariation**: how do two measurements vary *together*? How we look depends on
the types of the two variables.

## Joint and conditional distributions

For two variables $X$ and $Y$:

* The **joint distribution** says how often each combination $(X, Y)$ occurs.
* Fixing $X = x$ and looking at the $Y$ values gives a **conditional
  distribution** of $Y$ given $X = x$.

Conditional distributions are often easier to work with -- especially when we
condition on a categorical variable.

## Stratifying on a category

To condition on a (rounded) happiness rating, we **stratify** -- group by it --
and summarize the rating in each group:

```{r}
wae |>
  mutate(happy_round = round(`Art (image+title): happiness`, 1)) |>
  group_by(happy_round) |>
  summarize(median = median(`Ave. art rating`),
            mean   = mean(`Ave. art rating`))
```

A **violin plot** shows the whole conditional distribution in each stratum:

```{r}
wae |>
  mutate(happy_round = round(`Art (image+title): happiness`, 1)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = factor(happy_round), y = `Ave. art rating`)) + geom_violin()
```

## Two quantitative variables

When both variables are quantitative, start with a scatterplot; where points
overplot, a 2D histogram shows where the data piles up:

```{r warning = FALSE}
ggplot(wae, aes(x = year4_num, y = `Ave. art rating`)) + geom_bin2d()
```

## Conditional means by stratifying

We can condition a continuous $X$ by cutting it into intervals and taking the
**mean of $Y$** in each -- a set of conditional means:

```{r warning = FALSE}
wae |>
  mutate(year_cat = cut_width(year4_num, 100)) |>
  group_by(year_cat) |>
  summarize(mean_rating = mean(`Ave. art rating`))
```

## Smoothing: loess

Cutting into bins is clumsy. **Locally weighted regression** (loess) estimates
the conditional mean of $Y$ smoothly across $X$ -- a trend line that follows the
data:

```{r warning = FALSE}
ggplot(wae, aes(x = year4_num, y = `Ave. art rating`)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_smooth()
```

That smooth curve *is* an estimate of "the average rating, given the year."

## From description to models

A loess curve gave us conditional means without a formula. But we often want to
describe a relationship with a specific **number** -- a slope -- rather than a
picture, and to reason about it. For that we use **models**, which estimate the
**conditional mean**

$$E[Y \mid X = x] = \text{the average } Y \text{ among observations with } X = x.$$

To see modeling clearly, let's switch to a cleaner two-variable example: engine
size (`displ`) and highway mileage (`hwy`) in the `mpg` data.

## Linear regression

The workhorse is `lm()` (linear model). We give it a **formula**,
`response ~ predictor`, and a data frame:

```{r}
fit <- lm(hwy ~ displ, data = mpg)
fit
```

The formula `hwy ~ displ` reads "model highway mileage as a function of engine
displacement." `lm()` finds the line -- a conditional mean $\widehat{hwy} = b_0 +
b_1 \cdot displ$ -- that best fits the data.

## A fitted model is an object

Remember from the OOP lecture: everything in R is an object with a class. A
fitted model is no exception.

```{r}
class(fit)
```

It is an S3 object of class `"lm"` built on a list. When you print `fit` or call
`summary(fit)`, that is **method dispatch** -- R calls `print.lm()` and
`summary.lm()`, the same generics we have used all term, specialized for models.

## Tidy model output with `broom`

`summary(fit)` is made to be *read*, not *computed with*. The **`broom`** package
turns a model into tidy tibbles with three functions:

```{r}
tidy(fit)      # one row per coefficient
```

```{r}
glance(fit)    # one row of overall fit statistics
```

The slope from `tidy(fit)` says highway mileage drops by about 3.5 mpg for each
1-liter increase in displacement -- a single number summarizing the
relationship, exactly what EDA was reaching for.

## Predictions and residuals with `modelr`

The **`modelr`** package adds the model's view back onto the data as ordinary
columns: `add_predictions()` adds the fitted conditional mean, and
`add_residuals()` adds what the line missed (`actual - predicted`):

```{r}
mpg |>
  add_predictions(fit) |>
  add_residuals(fit) |>
  select(displ, hwy, pred, resid) |>
  head()
```

## Residuals send us back to EDA

The residuals are the leftovers. If the model captured the relationship, they
should look like featureless noise around 0 -- so we do **EDA on the
residuals**:

```{r}
mpg |>
  add_residuals(fit) |>
  ggplot(aes(displ, resid)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "grey60") +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE)
```

There is a clear **U-shape** left over: the line over- and under-predicts in a
systematic way. A straight conditional mean is too rigid here.

## When a line is not enough: polynomial regression

We can let the conditional mean **curve** while staying within `lm()`, by adding
a squared term with `poly()`:

```{r}
fit2 <- lm(hwy ~ poly(displ, 2), data = mpg)

mpg |>
  add_predictions(fit2) |>
  ggplot(aes(displ, hwy)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_line(aes(y = pred), color = "darkgreen", linewidth = 1)
```

This is still linear regression -- still `lm`, still a conditional mean we can
write as a formula -- but now it bends, and its residuals lose most of that
U-shape.

## loess again -- now as a model

We met **loess** earlier as an EDA smoother. It belongs here too: it estimates
the conditional mean *locally*, fitting a little regression near each $x$, with
no global formula at all. The `span` argument controls how smooth it is:

```{r}
ggplot(mpg, aes(displ, hwy)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", span = 0.75, se = FALSE, color = "red")
```

## Three views of one conditional mean

All three estimate $E[hwy \mid displ]$ -- they trade simplicity for flexibility:

```{r}
ggplot(mpg, aes(displ, hwy)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, aes(color = "1: linear")) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ poly(x, 2), se = FALSE, aes(color = "2: quadratic")) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", se = FALSE, aes(color = "3: loess")) +
  labs(color = NULL)
```

* **Linear**: one slope, easy to interpret and extrapolate, but can miss
  curvature.
* **Polynomial**: still a formula, bends to fit, but can behave wildly past the
  data.
* **loess**: follows the data closely with no formula, but is local -- it cannot
  predict outside the observed range.

## Exercise

Fit `lm(hwy ~ displ)` separately for each `drv` (drivetrain) using
`geom_smooth(method = "lm")` with `color = drv`. Does the relationship between
displacement and mileage look the same for all three drivetrains?

```{r drv-models, exercise = TRUE}

```

## Summary

* **EDA** is the informal, data-driven search for good questions: describe
  variation, then covariation.
* One variable: **counts/proportions** for categories; the **ECDF**,
  **histograms**, and **density plots** for quantitative data. A **proportion is
  the mean of a condition**.
* Two variables: **conditional distributions** via stratifying and violins;
  scatter and 2D histograms; **loess** gives a smooth conditional mean.
* A **model** estimates the **conditional mean** $E[Y \mid X]$: `lm()` fits a
  line (an S3 object); `broom` tidies its output and `modelr` adds
  predictions/residuals.
* **Residuals are EDA's feedback loop**; **polynomial regression** and **loess**
  give more flexible conditional means, trading interpretability for
  flexibility.

Reading: [R for Data Science (2e), "EDA"](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/eda) and
[(1e) "Model basics"](https://r4ds.had.co.nz/model-basics.html).
